
  She lit the wick. The lens gathered the small yellow flame and hurled it over the water.

  The whole apparatus floated on a trough of mercury, and a child's push could turn its four tons. As it revolved, the
  bullseyes swept their beams across the dark like spokes. From the sea, a sailor saw one flash every ten seconds, and
  that was how he knew this light from all the others.

  Tonight the fog came in thick from the southwest. Maren watched the beams grow solid in it, like white rafters turning
  overhead. Then, at a quarter past two, the turning stopped.

  She was up the stairs before she had fully woken. The weight chain had jammed with a kinked link, and the lens stood
  still, pouring one fixed beam uselessly toward the open sea. A fixed light was a lie, because it told a ship it was
  somewhere else.

  There was a ship. She had heard its horn an hour ago, low and uncertain, feeling its way toward the channel.

  Maren put her palms flat against the brass frame and pushed. The lens moved as easily as a door. She counted under her
  breath, walking the slow circle and finding the pace: a full turn in forty seconds, a flash every ten. Round and
  round the lamp she went, with the heat on her cheek and the prisms throwing coloured slivers across her hands.

  She walked for four hours. Her legs burned, then went numb, then seemed to belong to someone else. She counted the
  whole time.

  At dawn the fog thinned and showed her a freighter riding safely at anchor inside the bar. Its horn sounded twice,
  which she chose to take as thanks.

  Maren let the lens drift to rest, trimmed the wick, and drew the curtains against the sun so the glass would not
  gather daylight and set the tower alight. Then she went down to fix the chain.
